From the changing electric grid to a compact

Buxin She
Mike Wiegers Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering

Two views of the same power system
LECTURE STRUCTURE
Evolution and state of the art
how local grids became
interconnected networks;
why sensing, communication,
storage, and distributed resources
matter;
how generation mix and resource
geography shape operation.
Symbolic representation
how physical equipment becomes a
one-line diagram;
what each symbol preserves and
suppresses;
how buses, branches, injections,
and withdrawals form a solvable
model.
The grid keeps changing, but engineers still need a stable language for representing
connectivity and power flow.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 2/33

PART I
Power-System Evolution and State of the Art
How the grid grew, where electricity comes from, and why operation is
changing
Acknowledgment
This section is adapted primarily from Prof. Anil Pahwa’s
Electricity Access Challenge 2025 slides.

From local service to interconnection
POWER-SYSTEM EVOLUTION
1882: local DC service
Pearl Street served a compact
area in lower Manhattan.
1884: early AC
transmission
Transformers made
higher-voltage transfer
practical.
Today: interconnected
infrastructure
Power systems coordinate many
sources, networks, and users.
Increasing distance, scale, and interconnection created the need for common
equipment models and coordinated operation.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 4/33

National grid
CONTINENTAL-SCALE COORDINATION
NREL planning-study map of regional interfaces and candidate AC transmission expansion.
Bulk transmission links geographically separated resources and demand while
requiring planning across regional boundaries.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 5/33

Network reliability
STATE OF THE GRID
Why local failures can spread
power flows redistribute immediately
after an outage;
overloaded equipment and inadequate
visibility can create cascading events;
aging assets, extreme weather, cyber
risk, and changing generation add new
operating stress.
Reliability depends on the condition and
coordination of the whole interconnected
network.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 6/33

Smart-grid layers
SMART-GRID CONCEPT
Core capabilities
sensors make operating
conditions visible;
communication moves
measurements and
commands;
computation supports
estimation, protection,
optimization, and control.
“Smart” describes coordinated sensing, communication, and decision-making—not a
different physical law.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 7/33

Traditional and evolving grids
TRADITIONAL STRUCTURE AND EMERGING OPERATION
Traditional grid
Large central plants; mostly one-way delivery;
limited end-use visibility.
Evolving grid
Distributed energy, storage, communication, and
more active customers.
The same network must increasingly coordinate power that enters, exits, and changes
direction at many locations.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 8/33

Generation mix
UNITED STATES AND KANSAS
A national portfolio can be diverse even when an individual state relies heavily on a
particular local resource.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 9/33

Resource geography
RESOURCE GEOGRAPHY
Wind resource
 Solar resource
Resource maps help explain why new generation and new transmission do not appear
uniformly across the country.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 10/33

Variable generation and net load
FROM AVAILABLE ENERGY TO NET-LOAD RAMPS
PV output varies
 The system sees net load
Operators must balance demand minus variable generation continuously, including
steep ramps and forecast error.
ECE 685 | Power-System Overview 11/33

Bus

Bus meaning
Every terminal on one bus shares
the same voltage phasor.
A branch between buses permits
different voltage magnitudes or
angles.
The bus organizes connectivity; it
is not a storage tank for power.
One bus ID corresponds to one
electrical node and one solved
voltage.

Capacitor or reactor
A capacitor supplies reactive
power at its bus.
A reactor absorbs reactive
power at its bus.
Rating, status, and bus voltage
determine the operating effect.
Local shunt support can reduce
the reactive power carried by an
upstream branch.
